newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: American mining firm says Kabila rivals seize jet.
newsitem.headline: American mining firm says Kabila rivals seize jet.

text.p: A rival faction within Laurent Kabila's alliance in the new Democratic Republic of Congo had impounded a private jet leased by America Mineral Fields Inc in an attempt to embarrass the former rebel leader, the company said on Friday.

News reports said Kabila had seized the plane last month at Lubumbashi Airport after its pilot, kept waiting by Kabila for six hours, left without him for Zimbabwe. Kabila was due to fly to South Africa to meet President Nelson Mandela.
Kabila's democratic alliance ousted former Zaire President Mobutu Sese Seko in May. The jet, leased from a South African company by AMF, was lent to Kabila during his campaign.

"Within the alliance you're going to have factions. One of the factions at the airport got crosswires with the pilot and saw an opportunity to embarrass the president (Kabila)," Earl Young, AMF's senior vice president of finance, told Reuters.
"This is the plane lent to Kabila. It's been a month now and it's still sitting on the runway," he said.
Young said AMF would allow the government to solve the matter among themselves, adding that the company believed a solution was close at hand.

"It's a short time between now and when the plane is released. We are close to the government. We are friends to the people. We'll leave the president to work out a practical political solution to the problem," he said.
"We're not angry at the faction. We're not angry at the president -- They have a problem, they must sort it out."
Since Kabila seized control of the country, international mining companies have scrambled over each other to try to win mining contracts and exploration permits.

AMF was the first company to be awarded a mining project by the new government. In April it won the right to develop the Kolwezi copper/cobalt tailings project and to build a 200,000 tonne-a-year zinc smelter at Kipushi.
But the company has said it is not a favourite with Kabila.
"Some of the press has suggested that AMF came in on the coat-tails of the alliance. I want to stress that this is not so. We were first here about two years ago," said AMF director Richard Garnett.
Garnett was addressing a delegation of European and U.S. investors visiting the new Congo on the invitation of AMF.
Reports earlier this week also said that in a separate incident, soldiers at Lubumbashi Airport had seized core samples of rock which AMF was allegedly trying to smuggle out of the country.
"It was not samples, it was some equipment. Often with equipment there is problems bringing it in or taking it out," Young said, without giving details.
